questions.q: What does security.protocol=SASL_SSL actually turn on, according to this lesson?
options: It disables authentication entirely for faster connections
A single setting that has no relationship to encryption at all
Only authorization, with no effect on authentication or encryption
Two separate things at once: SASL authentication (who the client is) and SSL encryption (protecting data in transit)
questions.explain: SASL and SSL are two separate concerns bundled into one connection setting — one proves identity, the other protects the data on the wire.

questions.q: In this lesson's SASL_SCRAM config, why does the password appear as "${KAFKA_PASSWORD}" instead of a literal string?
options: Kafka requires all passwords to use that exact syntax or it won't parse the config
It's an environment variable, following the same secrets-handling discipline Git/GitHub/CI-CD Lesson 23 taught for any pipeline secret
It has no real purpose and could be replaced with a hardcoded password with no downside
Environment variables are only used for Kafka topic names, not passwords
questions.explain: Pulling the secret from an environment variable instead of hardcoding it keeps credentials out of the config file itself, the same practice covered in Git/GitHub/CI-CD Lesson 23.

questions.q: What do ACLs (Access Control Lists) actually control in Kafka, per this lesson?
options: What operations a specific, already-authenticated principal is allowed to perform on a specific resource, like a topic
Who is allowed to authenticate to the cluster at all
The number of partitions a topic can have
How data is encrypted in transit
questions.explain: ACLs are the authorization layer — they answer 'what can this identity do' after authentication has already answered 'who is this.'

questions.q: Why does this lesson's example grant orders-consumer Read access scoped to the specific group orders-processor, rather than an unscoped grant?
options: Scoping to a group has no security benefit over an unscoped grant
Kafka ACLs cannot be scoped to a consumer group at all
It enforces least privilege at the same granularity Lesson 8's consumer-group model already uses — this identity can only read as that one group
It grants access to every topic in the cluster automatically
questions.explain: Scoping the grant to one consumer group keeps the permission narrow — the identity can't use that read access as some other, unintended group.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe itself as covering security "basics," not a full deep-dive?
options: Because authentication, encryption, and authorization aren't actually necessary in production
Because real production Kafka security also covers things like audit logging, network isolation, and key rotation that go beyond one lesson's honest scope
Because Kafka has no additional security features beyond what's shown here
Because this lesson secretly covers everything needed for a fully secured production cluster
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that it's covering the three practical basics that have to be right first, not claiming to be an exhaustive security treatment.
